Farmers warn rising fuel costs are squeezing farm incomes

8th October 2026

Author: Aleksandra Cupriak

As fuel prices surged again this year, British farmers warned that rising input costs are not being matched by higher prices for local food producers, putting further pressures on farm businesses.

At the start of 2026, farmers buying a substantial volume of red diesel could expect to pay around 65–70p/litre. Prices then surged as the Middle East conflict disrupted global oil and fuel supplies, rising to more than £1.20/litre by April. 

Prices subsequently eased, falling to around 80p/litre by mid-June, but began rising again through the summer. By the end of July, red diesel was averaging about 98p/litre, increasing to 104.77p/litre in August and 112.95p/litre in September, according to AHDB. 

The latest rise has been linked to continued disruption in global diesel markets, including Middle East tensions and reduced Russian refinery output. 

Ben Aveling, who runs Radmore Farm in Northamptonshire, said the biggest issue farmers face is that they cannot simply pass the additional cost of diesel on to the price they receive for their produce.  

“As farmers, we’re often told what we’ll get for our produce, with prices driven by the market rather than what it costs us to produce it. Businesses further along the supply chain can put their prices up to cover higher transport and fuel costs.  

“But at the farm level, we don’t have that same freedom. We have to swallow those costs, which puts farms at an unfair disadvantage. That’s the squeeze we’re facing: our costs go up, but the price we’re paid doesn’t automatically rise with them. We’re expected to keep producing food without being able to pass those extra costs on.” 

Ben said that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine also led to higher costs, which fed through into food prices and were ultimately felt by consumers at the checkout.  

“Brands and retailers passed on some of those costs rather than absorbing them all. But as farmers, we can’t simply put our prices up because diesel costs more. The market still dictates what we’re paid.  

“That’s the difference: higher costs don’t automatically mean a higher price for our produce.” 

Eleanor Gilbert, who farms on her family’s Rookery Farms in Berkshire, added: “If you were already questioning whether you could afford to keep farming, the latest rise in fuel prices makes that question even harder to answer.” 

Eleanor said that last week alone, her family had to put £3,000 worth of diesel through just one tractor. “That’s one tractor in one week. And fuel is just one of the many rising costs we face as farmers. The question is no longer just how we can afford to farm, but whether we can afford to carry on farming at all.” 

‘We need to reduce our use of fossil fuels’

Martin Lines, Cambridgeshire farmer and CEO of the Nature Friendly Farming Network (NFFN), added: “These rising fuel prices are not a one-off event but merely the latest episode in months of volatility and price spikes due to geopolitical instability in the Middle East.” 

He said that, with no end to rising costs in sight, the situation once again underlines the urgent need for farming to reduce its reliance on fossil fuels. 

“Cutting down diesel and fertiliser use, accompanied by a transition to nature-friendly farming, should be a win-win for agricultural businesses: lower input and operating costs and greater protection against instability,” Martin explained. 

He continued: “At the same time, we all need to urgently reduce our use of fossil fuels, as without concerted action runaway climate change will make reliable food production almost impossible.  

“This summer, with its heatwaves and long drought, has already shown just how difficult climate change is making farming, and as it stands, this will be the coolest summer we will experience for the rest of our lives. All our futures, not just those of our farmers, rest on curbing emissions and switching, wherever possible, from fossil fuels to renewable energy.” 

Another blow for British farmers

NFU deputy president and Yorkshire farmer Paul Tompkins said: “Red diesel is the primary fuel for agricultural vehicles, which are crucial in producing the nation’s food. As fuel prices rise again due to geopolitical events, so does the financial strain for British farm businesses.” 

Paul added that these increasing costs come at an already incredibly difficult time for farmers and growers, with this summer’s drought having impacted cashflow and confidence. 

“We welcomed the government’s decision to freeze the planned rise in fuel duty earlier this year, but there are still steps that could be taken to ease financial pressures. This includes delaying the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) tax, one of five key priorities the NFU is urging the government to consider ahead of its upcoming Budget, to avoid adding further financial burden through higher fertiliser prices. 

“Farmers and growers are proud of the vital role they play in producing food for 29 million households, but with the right support and confidence to invest, we can build a more resilient and profitable farming sector and strengthen our national food security,” he concluded.
